162. Tablinum (15): through a small white marble threshold, the floor is slightly raised above the atrium. The centre is occupied by a large emblem in opus sectile of polychrome marble with a white marble border, and is further distinguished by the carpet of white tesserae arranged in an oblique warp by means of two edges also mosaic, with a two-strand braid and an acanthus shoot. 163. Tablinum (15): the central emblem in opus sectile of polychrome marbles.

164. Tablinum (15): detail of the border of the central emblem, in black and white mosaic. A low band with a two-strand braid is followed by a higher band, in which the motif of the branch populated by birds, which arises from an angular head of acanthus, is executed with a certain rigidity.

165. Tablinum (15), N wall: the decoration of the fourth style continues according to the same scheme as that of the atrium; In fact, a faux marble plinth is followed, in the middle area, by a large scenography that occupies the entire wall and emphasizes the importance of the central painting, inserted separately and embedded within a wooden frame with horizontal and vertical boards, of which the imprints are still recognizable. With regard to this circumstance, Bechi (MB, cited in bibl., p. 8) — referring to the practice of detaching paintings for transfer to museums, typical of his time — notes "that not only did the ancients know this industry of detaching and transporting the paintings of the cassocks from one wall to another, but that what is more important they used the same methods that we use,  since they cut the edges and enclosed them in wooden boxes, as Vitruvius (Lib. II chap. VII) and Pliny (Hist. Lib. XXXV chap. 49) have left us". The central panel has not been found.

166. Tablinum (15): on the S wall, on which the sun shines stronger, the decoration of the IV style has been preserved much worse than on the wall in front. It is possible to see here the heterogeneity of the materials and techniques used in the masonry (uncertain work with jambs in tuff and lava blocks mixed with brick or brick only resorts). IV style. 79 N51078
167. Tablinum (15), N wall, section O: detail of the forepart with coffered ceiling. IV style.

168. Triclinium (16): the overall view from the E allows us to reconstruct the relationship between this room and the wing in front of it (8), which forms a sort of spacious antechamber, accessible through the large opening on the W wall, from which it is also possible to grasp the view of the atrium (2). The flooring technique is the same in the two rooms, in mosaic

169. Triclinium (16). It is interesting to note that the room, which has neither on the floor nor on the wall scans of the decoration that suggest a triclinary use, was instead used as such, as would result from the discovery in it of "a piece of furniture with a cushion at the top (perhaps a long bench for sitting). The same was resting on eight feet covered with silver leaves, but very unpreserved. Other small bands in the form of bracelets, also made of silver, belonged to this piece of furniture" (PAH, II, p. 465). The triclinium use of the room is also evident from the subject of the large paintings that were placed in the center of the walls (see figs.  INS. 3, 5.24

170. Triclinium (16): the floor of the large room, which must have been flooded with light from both the large door and the large windows, is in black and white mosaic, adorned with a continuous motif — a network of double-T meanders — which makes it a large carpet. In the foreground, the marble threshold of access from the wing (8), with recessed luminaires that made it possible to close or screen the room.

171. Triclinium (16). In the table by G. Abbate (cfr. Disegnatori, p. 366, fig. 82) the rich decoration of the fourth style of the room is reproduced, with cinnabar walls occupied in the center by large-format paintings and smaller paintings in the side panels, all having subjects related to the theme of banINS. 3, 5.24

172. Triclinium (16), N wall with the large window with marble sill open onto the viridarium (18). The dimensions of the various elements of the IV style decoration are larger than normal, as they fit into those of the room. The plinth has large black "windows" with yellow foreparts; the middle area has a large painting with the triumph of Dionysus in the center, the only one left in situ of the decoration of the entire room. Between the central panel and the side panel (from which the painting has been detached: see fig. 169), there is a large architectural foreshortening seen from the front. The upper area is not decorated, and has only a layer of preparation that here was not intended to receive the painted decoration (the walls were in fact, in ancient times as today, from top to bottom), but rather to finish the masonry, which at this point could be covered by curtains.
173. Triclinium (16), N wall, section W: plinth with a large black 'window' adorned with a plant shoot; the high red band with meander decoration of the panel above is visible. IV style.
174. Triclinium (16): painting with cupids preparing for a tragic performance (H, 768; MNN, inv. 9191), detached from the side panel of this wall.
175. Triclinium (16), N wall, section O: architectural view with a flooded ceiling adorned with coffers and a hanging garland. IV style.
176. Triclinium (16), N wall, section O: Maenad dancing within the architectural foreshortening. IV style.
177. Triclinium (16), N wall, central section: in the black 'window' of the plinth is a scene of hunting among animals. IV style. 79 N50309

178. Triclinium (16), N wall, central section: painting with the triumph of Dionysus. The painting is the only one left in situ of the decoration of the room and, both as far as we can still judge and for what we read about it in the nineteenth-century comments, it seems to have been — like the other large paintings in the room — of decidedly higher quality than the average of the paintings found in Pompeii: this must be the reason that led Bechi to believe (cited in bibl.,  p. 9; cf. also H, 565) that the paintings had been transported here from another place [it should be remembered that a practice of this kind is attested on the walls of the tablinum (15), cf. figs. 165, 167]. The dimensions of the painting (156 x 194 cm) are however such as to suggest that Minervini is rather right (in MB, XV commentary on tavv. XVIII and XIX, pp. 7-8), Overbeck (cited in bibl., p. 318) and O. Donner (in H, pp. LXKX-LXXI), who instead considered the paintings executed în situ, within a specially prepared recess, the margins of which are clearly recognizable (Bechi, cit., however, states that he found the plaster of the walls and that of the paintings 'very different from each other' in their composition). On the reasons why this painting, unlike all the others in the environment, remained in situ, cf. G. Minervini's commentary on tav. XXXII, in MB, XV.

179. Triclinium (16). Niccolini's panel allows us to recognize the iconographic elements of the painting reproduced in fig. in which the trophy at the center of the composition, the Victory writing on the shield, the prisoner on the ground with his hands tied behind his back, are elements of a Hellenistic iconography of victory, taken from Roman imperial art.
180. Triclinium (16), N wall, central section: detail of the head of Dionysus, with thyrsus and crown of vine leaves.
181. Triclinium (16), N face, central section: detail of the trophy.
182. Triclinium (16), N wall, central section: detail of the prisoner on the ground.
183. Triclinium (16), N wall, central section: the figure of Nike noting the victories on the shield is now almost unrecognizable.
184. Triclinium (16), N wall, section E: black 'window' with branch; band with meander edge. IV style.
185. Triclinium (16), wall E: the remains left in situ of the decoration of the IV style.

186. Triclinium (16), wall E, section N: plinth with a black 'window' adorned with a floral branch and a band with a meander border of the middle area. Both the branch and the meander were carried out with the help of guide lines. IV style.

187. Triclinium (16), wall E, section N: yellow frame and meander band, executed with the help of horizontally engraved guide lines; The pattern is rarely present in contemporary decorations due to the time it takes to make it. IV style.

188. Painting with cupids and Psychai at an outdoor banquet, under a tent erected in front of a statue of Dionysus (H, '759; MNN, inv. 9207); The cupid in the foreground carries the wine amphora, the one on the left plays the lyra, the couple on the right is 'in conversation', everyone wears crowns on their heads. Diap. AFSN s.n.
189. Triclinium (16), wall E, central section: forepart with Satyr playing the double flute. IV style.
190. Triclinium (16), wall E, central section: plinth with black 'window' with wild boar hunted by dogs (reproduced in MB, XIV, tav. XLIV). IV style. 79 N50320

19la-d. Triclinium (16): in the centre of the wall E the power of Dionysus is symbolised by the painting reproduced here (H, 1140; MNN, inv. 8992): Heracles, abandoning the club and the skin of the lion and dressed civilly and even luxuriously (like Dionysus) — even if the rich purple robe with a green border makes his powerful body stand out more than it covers it — wears the crown of the banquet and advances drunkenly leaning on Priapus, while on the right Omphales, leaning on the thyrsus of the Maenad,  He wears the club, and the lion's skin, of the hero. It is a theme that we know in Pompeii in various forms: summarized only by the busts of the couple and recognizable because Omphales wears the skin of a lion (cf. for example H, 1134; cf. MNN, inv. 9004: Collections, pp. 160 s., no. 263), in a redaction with Hercules enthroned (cf. for example House of Hercules, VI 7, 6: vol. IV, pp. 374-376, fig. 9), or in a more 'playful' version, such as that of the painting from the Excavation of the Prince of Montenegro (VII 16, 10, cf. vol. VII, p. 841, fig. 2) or,  as in this painting, in a realization of great technical and stylistic quality and of high structure, similar to that present on the N wall of the same room (see fig. 178). The height of the iconographic conception also results here from the way in which the hero is dressed: from the disguise with Omphales' robes emerges the awareness of the value of civilizing signs (the luxury of clothes and behavior) in the construction of the meaning of the figure and the scene. Diap. AFSN s.n.; from Niccolini, Taw. VIII - X (Fot. Rossini)

192. Triclinium (16), wall E, section S: plinth with black 'window' with branch. IV style.
193. Triclinium (16). Painting with cupids and Psychai at an outdoor banquet, on the sigma-shaped cushion, in front of a statue of Heracles (H, 757; MNN, inv. 9255) from the S side panel.

194. Triclinium (16), S wall: masonry with tuff blocks alternating with bricks, high windows and rough plaster in the upper area (see fig. 172). Yellow forepart plinth with black 'windows', separated by compartments with figures; from the red middle area (cinnabar?) the three paintings of figs. 196, 199, 202. IV style.
195. Triclinium (16), S wall, section E: plinth with black window adorned with branches; yellow frame and band with meander. IV style.
196. Painting with cupids preparing a dramatic chorus (H, 767; MNN, inv. 9193).

197. Triclinium (16), S wall, section E: painting with architectural foreshortening representing a flooded roof adorned with wooden coffers, represented in a frontal view; a double-arched garland hangs from the roof, in the center is a dancing Maenad. IV style.
198. Triclinium (16), S face, central section: the paradeisos of the plinth is now completely lost on this wall. IV style.

199. Triclinium (16): painting with the triumph of Dionysus as a child, surrounded by his retinue and held in Silenus' arms, on a cart pulled by two oxen (H, 379; MNN, inv. 9285). This painting, like the other two in the room, was executed within a recess specially made in the plaster, as Overbeck rightly believes (cited in the bibl., p. 318) against the opinion of those, from Bechi to Helbig (bibl. cit. in fig. 178), who believed that the painting had been executed separately (or detached from another site?) and then inserted into the wall.
200. Triclinium (16), S wall, section O: compartment with a yellow background (flushed in red due to the effect of heat) in the plinth. IV style.
201. Triclinium (16), S wall, section O, detail of fig. Previous: Egyptian female figure (offerer with patera in the left and sistrum in the right). IV style.
202. Triclinium (16): painting with cupids preparing a lyric chorus (H, 766; MNN, inv. 9206).
203. Triclinium (16), W wall, S section: plinth with black 'window' with branch; edge with meander band. IV style.

204. Fauces (17), view from the W: the staircase, with a brick tread, connects the level of the parts of the house seen so far to the highest level of the area behind, the garden with the living rooms overlooking it and the adjoining house with entrance at no. 24. It is therefore a service area, but located in the heart of the residential area, and the decoration reflects this function: the scheme is in fact rather simple, but does not renounce the figurative element — albeit in the form of simple vignettes, which also allude to various deities.
205. Fauces (17): remains of decoration of the fourth style (upper white area with architecture).
206. Fauces (17), N wall, section O: black plinth and red middle area with panel bordered by carpet edges. IV style.
207. Fauces (17), detail of fig. previous: vignette with the attributes of Zeus (H, 111): the globe, the protome of Zeus and the eagle.
208. Reproduction of the vignette in fig. previous. from MB, XIV, Tav. XLIV (Fot. Rossini)
209. Fauces (17), N wall, central section: aedicule with gilded candelabrum in the red middle area. IV style.

210. Fauces (17), wall N, section E: the state of conservation of the decoration of the IV style does not allow us to say with certainty that the vignette reproduced here is the one with the attributes of Aphrodite (H, 302, vase adorned with a dolphin and female protome).

211. Fauces (17), S face, section E: red middle area; panel with vignette and carpet borders. The attributes of Heracles (H, 1121) are perhaps represented in the vignette: pig, club, protome of Heracles. IV style.
212. Fauces (17), S wall, central section: aedicule with a red background with a gilded candelabrum. IV style.
213. Fauces (17), S face, O section: black plinth; red middle area with panel with vignette with Hera's attributes, and carpet edges. IV style.

214. In the reproduction of N. The Fox in the cartoon of fig. The elements listed in H, 167 can be recognized: the protome of Hera (?) with radiated crown and the peacock (cf. Disegnatori, p. 598, fig. 32).

215. Viridarium (18) (see the old photo on fig. 161, with the rich statuary furnishings, now removed): the fountain with a niche adorned with painted fish on a blue background and a row of stucco shells, above which is the polychrome mosaic covering of the basin, depicting a shell; from the steps covered with white marble the water — gushing from a statuette of Silenus found here on May 12, 1847 (PAHI, II, p. 464) — flowed into another central circular fountain.
216. Viridarium (18): detail of the niche-fountain with painted decoration of swimming fish on a blue background. IV style.

217. Viridarium (18): the cap of the niche, adorned with a row of shells, above which the polychrome glass mosaic covering still pretends to be a large shell occupying the basin of the niche. IV style.
218. Viridarium (18): the circular masonry basin covered with marble, with a fountain jet in the centre, into which the water flowing down from the niche-fountain flowed.

219. Viridarium (18), N wall, O section: in the section of the wall adjacent to the tablinum you can recognize a painted garden, of which the plants behind the reed can barely be distinguished. The painting therefore completed and amplified the space of the royal garden, crowded with decorative sculptures, all linked to the theme of nature. IV style.
220. Viridarium (18), N wall, section O: detail of the garden painted with reed. IV style.

221. Viridarium (18): portico E with pillars and pluteus in opus incertum: a portion of plaster has been detached from the right pillar, most likely the one with the graffiti depicting the labyrinth and the inscription Labyrinthus hic habitat Minotaurus (CIL 2331, tav. XXXVIII, 1).

222. Viridarium (18), portico E: on the pluteus remains of a fresco with a reed. The decoration of this area also included "a garden with gates, in the middle of which is a large lake, on each side of it a swan, and on both sides of the garden a group of wrestlers with masks in the middle instead of herms to indicate the gymnasium" (Panofka, cited in bibl., p. 132). IV style.
223. Viridarium (18). Fragment of plaster with graffiti depicting the labyrinth and inscription (reproduction of N. La Volpe: cfr. Draftsmen, p. 597, fig. 31).
224. Room (19): cocciopesto floor. 79 N51122

225. Room (19), N wall: red plinth (panels with plants separated by foreparts with patera); flushed middle area (panels with carpet edges separated by architectural glimpses on a white background, closed by red partitions); the decoration of this room also included a painting with Paris and Helen (H, 1312). IV style.

226. Room (19), wall E: panels with plants and forepart with patera in the red plinth; flushed middle area (panel with carpet edges and architectural foreshortening on a white background closed by a red partition). IV style.
227. Room (19), wall E, section N: in the center of the panel only the shadow of a

228. Room (19), S wall, section E, with the square window open onto the viridarium: in the red plinth there are panels with large tufts of plants, separated by foreparts with patera; In the center of the middle area, around the window space, the architectural views closed by red partitions and the side panels with vignettes are symmetrically arranged. IV style.
229. Room (19), wall S, section O: the section of wall symmetrical to the one reproduced in fig. previous. IV style. 79 N51113
230. Room (19), S wall, section O: vignette with cupid armed on shelf. IV style. 79 N51116
231. Room (20): remains of the cocciopesto floor. 79 N51123

232. Room (20), wall N: the fourth style decoration of the room — if compared with that of the rooms at the front of the house — certainly does not appear particularly cared for, which makes it unlikely that the small picture detached from this wall (see fig. 234) was intended to allude to the owner of the house. In the center of the yellow plinth is a panel with a hanging mask, on the sides edges of a triangle carpet; the white middle area has a winged aedicule in perspective, flanked by compartments with a vegetable candelabra.
233. Room (20), N wall, central section: mask hanging in the plinth. IV style. 79 N51121

234. From room (20) comes the famous small picture with instrumentum scriptorium detached from the N wall, central section: open tablet, spatula, inkwell and quill, and the closed letter on which the heading M(arco) Lucretio Flam(ini) Martis Decurioni Pompei(s?) was read, from which the name given to the house derives (H, 1722; MNN, inv. 9818; CIL 879; cf. also Disegnatori, p. 347, figs. 159-158). Diap. AFSN s.n.
236. Room (20), wall O: the decoration takes up the same pattern as the wall in front. IV style.

235. Room (20), wall E: yellow plinth with central forepart with hanging mask and square carpet edges; white middle area with a panel bordered by carpet edges, in front of which there is an architectural view with a candelabra. IV style.

237. Triclinium (21), N wall with recessed bed: remains of white plaster. According to nineteenth-century reports (cf. Bechi, cited in bibl., p. 14) in the wall covering of this room there was an area with a simple white plaster covering, intended to be covered by curtains. The floor, like that of the viridarium, was made of cocciopesto with scattered marble flakes (Breton 1870, p. 394).

238. Triclinium (21), wall E: white plaster in the room and remains of a fresco of the fourth style with a symmetrical scheme in the antechamber, which has a narrow compartment with a candelabrum in the center and a panel on the sides that contained a now detached painting (it is uncertain whether it depicted Narcissus or, as Panofka records, in BdI, 1847, p. 132, Venus wearing the arms of Mars:  cf. H, 304); on the sides panels with medallions. In front of the wall, drums of fluted Ionic columns in tuff.
239. Triclinium (21), wall E, section S: the medallion with bust, depicted in the red panel of the middle area, is completely lost. IV style.
240. Triclinium (21), S wall: remains of a fresco of the fourth style of which only a few traces can now be distinguished.
242. Triclinium (21), S wall, section O: medallion with bust now completely vanished. IV style.
241. Triclinium (21), S wall, section E: medallion with bust now completely vanished. IV style.

243. Triclinium (21): in the centre of the wall reproduced in fig. 240 was this painting, of very mediocre quality, depicting Daphne transforming herself into a laurel to escape Apollo; the painting (H, 207) is now in the Museum of Naples (inv. 9536; cf. also Disegnatori, p. 515, fig. 32).

244. Room (22), N wall: fresco of the fourth style with a yellow background. The middle area has an aedicule in the center that contained a painting that is now illegible, on the sides panels with vignettes depicting cupids; in the upper white area there are figures within architecture. From Falkener (cited in the bibl., p. 80) we know that the cocciopesto floor had a rare ornamentation outlined in white tesserae: the rhombuses with the effect of perspective cubes (but it is not clear how the linear ornamentation could render a motif in perspective).
245. Room (22), N wall, section O: upper white area with figure inside an aedicule. IV style. 79 N50449
246. Room (22), N wall, section E: upper white area with figure inside an aedicule. IV style.
247. Room (22), wall E with illegible remains of frescoes, belonging to the same decorative phase depicted on wall N.

248. Exedra (25), view from the N: remains of a fresco of the fourth style with a white background. The decoration of the room was completed by predellas and friezes with cupids intent on various activities: after the detachment of these parts (of which the signs are clearly visible) the room was not protected and the wall and floor decoration is practically lost. 249. Exedra (25): remains of the black and white mosaic floor with a carpet of white tesserae arranged in an oblique warp, a border with black and white bands and a marginal flounce of black tesserae arranged in an oblique warp. The central element of the floor has not been found (cf. Bechi, cited in bibl., p. 13, who however speaks of a black meander edge, while in situ only the angular palmette and the wolf's tooth edge can be recognized today). The floor layout is contemporary to that of the other rooms with mosaic flooring in this house.

250. Exedra (25), wall O: remains of fresco of the fourth style. Also on this wall are clearly visible the signs left by the detachment of the ornaments with cupids harvesting (H, 801), which must therefore have occupied, as in the wall reproduced in fig. 248, the lower part of the middle area.
251. Exedra (25): in the fragment in the Museum of Naples (inv. 9338), coming from the lower part of the white middle area, they are cupids harvesting.

252. Exedra (25): in this fragment (MNN, inv. 9198) the cupids climb a ladder to harvest the bunches of the garland that delimits the middle area at the bottom; to the right of the fragment is the base of the vegetable candelabra that must have delimited the panel laterally; the ornaments are attributable to the IV style.
253. Exedra (25): frieze with children playing (H, 1477; MNN, inv. 9103; cf. also Disegnatori, p. 473, fig. 57).
254. Room (26): staircase leaning against wall E, resting on an arch in limestone blocks. 79 N50407

255. Room (27), W side: the wall, which is part of the house with entrance at no. 24, had a plastered niche, which was subsequently filled in by mixing fragments of cocciopesto with the masonry, and then covered with rough plaster.
256. Atrium (29), N wall, section O: remains of a fresco of the fourth style with a black plinth and a red middle area in which a band with carpet edges can be recognized.

The current condition of the painting allows us to recognize only part of what was seen at the time of the excavation. On the right sits the goddess with a high-rayed crown, short chiton and boots, next to her quiver and javelins; a Love with large wings rests on her knees. Behind her are two companions, also crowned and one with two javelins on which she leans, bowing her head; in front of Artemis you can see the remains of the standing figure of Kallistò with a short chiton, with hunter's boots, turquoise and bow on his shoulders. The figure of Kallistò was interpreted by the first exegetes as male, and Knapp, who was the first to describe her, even saw her bearded, a detail denied in the footnote, in the same place (Bd, 1879, pp. 108-109) by Mau.
